question: Let $y = \sin\left(n \sin^{-1} x\right),\ n \in \mathbb{N}$. For $|x| < 1$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + n^2y = $ ?
explanation:
Let $y = \sin(n \sin^{-1} x)$

Let $\theta = \sin^{-1} x$, so $y = \sin(n \theta)$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = n \cos(n\theta)\cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$

$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = n \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\cos(n\theta)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\right)$

$= n\left( -n\sin(n\theta) \cdot \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} + \cos(n\theta) \cdot \dfrac{x}{(1-x^2)^{3/2}} \right )$

$= -n^2 \sin (n\sin^{-1} x) \cdot \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} + n \cos(n\sin^{-1}x) \dfrac{x}{(1-x^2)^{3/2}}$

Thus,

$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + n^2y = n \cos(n \sin^{-1} x) \dfrac{x}{(1-x^2)^{3/2}}$
